title: FOMC Minutes — January 28–29, 2025
html:
Official minutes: HTML · PDF Local PDF: 2025-01-29 FOMC Minutes.pdf

Decision

The Committee held the federal funds target range at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent. Interest on reserve balances stayed at 4.4 percent and the primary credit rate at 4.5 percent. The vote was unanimous, 12-0: Powell, Williams, Barr, Bowman, Collins, Cook, Goolsbee, Jefferson, Kugler, Musalem, Schmid and Waller. Balance sheet runoff continued unchanged, with monthly caps of $25 billion for Treasuries and $35 billion for agency debt and MBS.

Economic outlook

Staff said real GDP rose at a solid pace in 2024 and in the fourth quarter, with private domestic final purchases likely growing faster than GDP. Participants agreed the economy kept expanding at a solid pace and that consumer spending was stronger than expected. Business investment in equipment and intangibles had been strong over the past year but appeared to slow in Q4. Some participants pointed to financial strain among low- and moderate-income households and to difficulties in agriculture.

Inflation

Total PCE inflation was 2.4 percent in November, down from 2.7 percent a year earlier; core PCE was 2.8 percent, down from 3.2 percent. Staff estimated December's 12-month figures at 2.6 percent total and 2.8 percent core. Staff projected 2025 inflation near 2024's pace, then a decline to 2 percent by 2027, with trade policy noted as an upward pressure. Participants said longer-term inflation expectations remained well anchored, though some market and survey measures had risen.

Labor market

Unemployment edged down to 4.1 percent in December. Payroll gains averaged about 170,000 per month over the last three months of 2024. Average hourly earnings growth slowed to 3.9 percent over the year, and the vacancies-to-unemployed ratio was 1.2. The picture was of a solid, gradually cooling job market.

Financial markets & balance sheet

Longer-dated Treasury yields rose 15 to 20 basis points over the intermeeting period and nearly 100 basis points since mid-September 2024. Credit spreads stayed very tight. Reserves were described as abundant, but the debt limit could cloud the signals: once it is resolved, reserves could fall quickly. Several participants said it might be appropriate to consider pausing or slowing runoff until the debt-limit situation was resolved. Staff also briefed on how the Treasury portfolio's maturity mix should look after runoff ends, and many favored eventually aligning it with outstanding Treasury debt.

Risks participants flagged

  • Upside inflation risks from changes in trade and immigration policy, including tariffs; firms said they would try to pass on tariff-related cost increases.
  • Supply-chain disruption from geopolitics and stronger household spending.
  • Downside risks to activity from an unexpected labor-market weakening, strained household finances or tighter financial conditions.
  • Financial stability: elevated asset valuations, nonbank leverage, commercial real estate, cyber risks and Treasury market dealer capacity.

What it signaled about next moves

Participants said the Committee was well positioned to wait and assess incoming data, wanting to see "further progress on inflation before making additional adjustments" as long as the economy stayed near maximum employment. Policy was "not on a preset course." Many said rates could stay restrictive if the economy stayed strong and inflation elevated; easing could follow if the labor market weakened or inflation fell faster. Market pricing was broadly consistent with one quarter-point cut in 2025.

Read-through for SPY

  • A patient, on-hold Fed meant no near-term rate relief; equity upside depended on earnings rather than lower rates.
  • Rising long-term yields and talk of tariff-driven inflation were a headwind for richly valued stocks.
  • The unanimous vote and solid-growth assessment lowered recession fears, a supportive backdrop for the broad market.
